bib.title: Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners" (KnowNo). Allen Z. Ren, Anushri Dixit, Alexandra Bodrova, Sumeet Singh, Stephen Tu, Noah Brown, Peng Xu, Leila Takayama, Fei Xia, Jake Varley, Zhenjia Xu, Dorsa Sadigh, Andy Zeng, Anirudha Majumdar. Princeton / Google DeepMind. arXiv:2307.01928v2 [cs.RO], 4 Sep 2023 (CoRL 2023 per the usual record; the extraction shows only the arXiv stamp, so venue is unconfirmed).

COVERAGE: 24 pages, 95,709 chars. I read the main text (pp. 1-9), the appendices A1-A9 and the Fig. A10/A11 captions in full. The reference list (pp. 10-13) was skimmed for origins. Extraction is usable. pypdf printed "FloatObject" warnings, which are harmless. The tail of A9 and a few baseline prompt listings (Fig. A5/A6) were skimmed only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: KnowNo has an LLM propose candidate next steps as multiple choice. It scores them by next-token probability and uses conformal prediction (CP) to keep a prediction set. If the set is a singleton the robot acts, otherwise it asks a human.
  number: none (mechanism)
  setup: PaLM-2L by default. Four generated options plus "an option not listed here". Few-shot generation, then a zero-shot letter-probability query.
  quote: "If there is more than one option in the set, the robot asks for help." / "If C(x̃test) is a singleton, the robot executes the corresponding plan. Otherwise, we deem the LLM uncertain over possible actions and trigger human help."
  where: p.2 (Fig. 1), p.5

- claim: With probability 1-δ over the calibration sample, the task completion rate is at least 1-ε, so the user chooses a success level and asking is calibrated to it. This also holds across multiple steps, via a sequence-level score (the minimum over steps), causally reconstructed.
  number: calibration N = 400, δ = 0.01
  setup: the guarantee holds only if the human help is faithful, the objects are fully grounded in the text, and low-level actions execute. It does not depend on how accurate or calibrated the LLM is.
  quote: "In practice, we use a modest-sized calibration dataset (N = 400) and δ = 0.01" / "We emphasize that the CP coverage guarantees hold regardless of the accuracy of f̂."
  where: p.4 (Sec 3.1), Props 1-2 pp.5-6

- claim: Against a threshold on the same LLM probabilities, KnowNo cuts human help by 10-24% at the same success level.
  number: 10-24%; 14% step-wise and 8% trial-wise (hardware tabletop); 14% (mobile manipulation)
  setup: the baseline (Simple Set) is given a larger ε so that plan success matches. The 24% figure is the best case, in the most ambiguous (Spatial) simulation setting, "at certain success levels".
  quote: "reducing human help by 10−24% compared to baseline approaches that lack formal assurances." / "KNOWNO reduces the human help rate by 14% step-wise and 8% trial-wise" / "as much as 24% at certain success levels."
  where: p.9 (Sec 6), p.8, p.7

- claim: Hardware tabletop, multi-step (UR5, sorting toy food). KnowNo hits the target trial-level success. Simple Set needs a much higher ε to match, and at the same ε it is hugely over-conservative.
  number: Table 1: KnowNo 1-ε 0.75, plan succ 0.76, task succ 0.74, set size 1.72, help-step 0.58, help-trial 0.92. Simple Set 0.58 / 0.76 / 0.72 / 2.04 / 0.72 / 1.00. No Help plan succ 0.41, task succ 0.38. Simple Set at ε=0.25 gives 87% step-wise help.
  setup: 50 hardware trials, ε=0.25 for KnowNo, ε=0.42 for Simple Set, PaLM-2L.
  quote: "KNOWNO 0.75 0.76 0.74 1.72 0.58 0.92" / "the planner is grossly over-conservative and requires a step-wise help rate of87%."
  where: p.7-8

- claim: Mobile manipulator in an office kitchen (Winograd-style and unsafe-action ambiguities). KnowNo asks less than Simple Set at the same plan success. No Help is much worse.
  number: Table 2: KnowNo 1-ε 0.85, plan 0.87, task 0.76, set size 2.22, help 0.67. Simple Set 0.76 / 0.87 / 0.75 / 2.38 / 0.81. No Help plan 0.62, task 0.51. Low-level action success is about 86%.
  setup: ε=0.15 for KnowNo, ε=0.24 for Simple Set, single-step, multiple acceptable answers.
  quote: "KNOWNO PaLM-2L 0.85 0.87 0.76 2.22 0.67" / "we find the low-level action success rate to be around 86%, which causes the non-trivial discrepancies between plan success and task success"
  where: p.8, p.23

- claim: Asking is useful beyond ambiguity because it covers unsafe actions. The motivating example is a metal bowl in a microwave. Unsafe instructions are one of the seven scenario types.
  number: none
  setup: scenario distribution in A7 (instruction types 1-7)
  quote: "Rather than acting in this ambiguous setting and damaging the microwave or even causing a fire, the robot should know when it doesn't know and ask for clarification instead"
  where: p.1

- claim: Prompt-only uncertainty (Prompt Set, Binary "Certain/Uncertain") gives no control over success rate. Prompt Set is worst. In the Spatial setting Prompt Set reaches only 35% task success.
  number: 35%
  setup: simulation tabletop, 200 trials per method and setting, ε=0.15 for the deviation plot (Fig. 3)
  quote: "Prompt Set does not show up in the human help rate plot for the Spatial setting as it only achieves 35% task success." / "Prompt Set performs the worst, indicating the challenge of prompting-based methods for calibrated prediction sets."
  where: p.7, p.23

- claim: A 20-sample ensemble can work well but costs 20x inference. It can also assign zero probability to the correct option, so it stops improving.
  number: 20x
  setup: ensemble of 20 randomized few-shot prompts
  quote: "it requires 20× inference time compared to other methods."
  where: p.7

- claim: Scoring whole sentences, instead of one multiple-choice letter, is worse. The gap grows with option-length variance.
  number: Numeric setting (length variance 8.51): KnowNo set size 2.17 and help 0.79, versus raw-probability CP at 4.06 and 1.00. Attribute: KnowNo help 0.18 versus 0.32 (raw) and 0.36 (perplexity).
  setup: simulation, ε=0.15
  quote: "CP w/ RawProb 4.06 1.00" / "using either sentence-level score leads to worse performance, and performance degradation correlates with variance of the multiple choice lengths."
  where: p.22 (Table A1)

- claim: The guarantee survives a weaker LLM. GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) has strong letter bias, so KnowNo compensates by asking more (set size 2.50, help 0.86). Instruction-finetuned PaLM-2L gives smaller sets (1.86) at the same help.
  number: GPT-3.5 set size 2.50, help 0.86; PaLM-2L-IF set size 1.86
  setup: Table 2 setting, no hardware run for these two models
  quote: "it exhibits significant MCQA bias towards options D and E and against A and B" / "KnowNo flexibly compensates for the degraded LLM performance by triggering more human intervention."
  where: p.8

- claim: Bimanual: when every instruction is ambiguous, help is frequent.
  number: 84% plan success at 92% help, ε=0.15. 9 of 10 trials succeeded, with help triggered 9 times.
  setup: Kuka bimanual, arm-reachability ambiguity, 10 trials
  quote: "the robot achieves 84% plan success with92% help. With 10 trials, the robot succeeds 9 times while triggering help for 9 times."
  where: p.16 (A5)

- claim: Labeling cost for calibration is hours of human work.
  number: about 4 hours for 400 multi-step examples, 1.5 hours for single-step
  quote: "Labeling the calibration data takes about 4 hours (for 400 examples) in the multi-step setting and 1.5 hours in single-step settings."
  where: p.6

LIMITS (authors' own, plus gaps)
- The guarantee assumes the environment is fully grounded in the LLM's text input and that proposed actions can be executed. Perception and low-level policy uncertainty are not modelled.
- It requires the human to "faithfully provide help"; human error is not modelled. Experiments use a simulated or idealised human.
- Fine-tuned prompt baselines were not made to work. Fine-tuned GPT-3 davinci overfit, so stronger fine-tuned Binary or Prompt Set baselines are untested.
- Calibration needs about 400 i.i.d. labelled scenarios from the deployment distribution, and a distribution shift voids the guarantee. The paper leaves it as a vision that a robot collects this with the end user.
- The scenarios are small and hand-built (blocks, toy food, kitchen items). The paper gives no test on long-horizon open-ended agents, tool-calling or coding. Hardware runs use 50 trials or fewer.
- Human help is counted as a rate, not a cost: there is no user study of fatigue or annoyance.
- Dated: PaLM-2L, GPT-3.5 davinci, and logit access are assumed. The method needs next-token probabilities, which many APIs now hide.
- Open-ended asks are left to future work. The question is generated from the prediction set.

BUILDS ON: Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer 2005 and Angelopoulos and Bates 2023 (conformal prediction). Vovk 2012 (dataset-conditional guarantee). Sadinle, Lei and Wasserman 2019 (least ambiguous sets). Kuhn et al. (semantic uncertainty, ref [38]). Kumar et al. (CP on MCQA). Ahn et al. 2022 (SayCan). Huang et al. 2022 (Inner Monologue, the prompt-based "ask" baseline). Liang et al. 2022 (Code as Policies). Lu et al. 2021 (ensemble over few-shot order). Guo et al. 2017 (miscalibration).

CODE: none worth keeping. Two prompt designs are verbatim:
- The multiple-choice query ends with "We: Which option is correct? Answer with a single letter." after options A-E, where one option is "an option not listed here" (Fig. A2, p.18).
- Algorithm 1 (p.14): "for time t←0 to T −1 do / Observe input x_t and predict the set C(x_t) / if C(x_t) is a singleton then Execute the action / else Ask for human help".

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.2): the bowl-in-microwave example. Option scores 0.44 and 0.41 are both above the 0.21 threshold, so the set has size 2 and the robot asks. This is the quickest picture of the ask rule.
- Fig. 2 (p.3): the calibration pipeline (MCQA, nonconformity scores, quantile).
- Fig. 3 (p.6): deviation from the target success rate per method.
- Fig. 4 (p.7): success vs set size and vs human-help rate, the main efficiency result.
- Fig. A10 (p.23): the same, split by ambiguity type.
- Fig. A11 (p.24): sampled kitchen scenarios where KnowNo returns a singleton and Simple Set returns a larger set.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from spacing artefacts ("W e", "T able"). Equation symbols are partly garbled, so I quoted the prose and tables instead. The venue is not printed in the extraction. The note's current text (04-execution-boundaries.md, search to ask to act, "when to ask") does not cite this paper. Most relevant here: the numbers apply to a calibrated single-step or per-step ask trigger on a multiple-choice proposal, not to LLM self-reported "uncertain" flags. The paper's Binary baseline (prompted Certain/Uncertain) is the one that lacks control and a guarantee.
